weekly-availability-editor.what: A form where each day of the week can be switched on or off and given one or more time ranges. It sets when a place is open or a person is available.
uses: Setting a shop's opening hours.
Letting staff or contractors set when they can work.
Defining when a service accepts bookings.
Setting a recording or maintenance schedule.
avoid: Single dates such as holidays: use a separate list of exceptions.
Hours that are the same every day: use a simpler start and end form.
practices: Allow several time ranges per day for lunch breaks and split shifts.
Show errors such as overlapping or reversed times on the row they affect.
Show the timezone the hours apply to.
Offer a shortcut to copy one day's hours to others.

working-hours-editor.what: A short form for regular working hours: which days, one start and end time, an optional break and a timezone. It suits hours that repeat every working day.
uses: Setting a person's standard working week.
Defining a team's core hours.
Setting default hours for a new account or location.
avoid: Hours that differ by day: use a day-by-day editor.
One-off changes like holidays: use an exceptions list.
practices: Preselect the most common days and times.
Write the result out in words so people can check it.
Always ask for or show the timezone.
Link to a per-day option for unusual weeks.

recurrence-editor.what: A control for making an event, task or report repeat. People pick how often, on which days and when it stops, and see the rule in plain words.
uses: Repeating meetings or appointments.
Scheduling recurring tasks and reminders.
Setting up reports that send on a schedule.
Repeating payments or deadlines.
avoid: Events that happen once: a plain date picker is enough.
Irregular dates that follow no pattern: list the dates individually.
practices: Offer common presets such as daily or weekly before a custom option.
Summarise the rule in a sentence, for example 'Every 2 weeks on Monday'.
Show the next few dates so mistakes are easy to spot.
Always give a clear way to end the repeat.

exception-editor.what: A list of dates that break from the usual schedule, such as holidays, closures or short days, with a way to add another.
uses: Listing public holidays and closing days.
Setting special opening hours for an event or season.
Recording planned absences of a person or place.
avoid: Changing the regular weekly pattern: edit the regular hours instead.
Recurring changes: use a repeat rule.
practices: Sort by date and hide past entries by default.
Show the date prominently and the reason beside it.
Offer to import public holidays for the user's country.
Let people edit or remove an entry in one step.

time-off-editor.what: A form for requesting leave, shown with the person's remaining balance and their existing requests. It can also let managers approve or decline.
uses: Requesting holiday, sick leave or training days.
Managers approving or declining leave.
Showing a person's leave history and balance.
avoid: Rostering who works when: use a schedule or roster view.
Recording hours worked: use a timesheet.
practices: Show the remaining balance and how many days the request uses before sending.
Support half days at the start and end.
Show each request's status clearly, with a word and not only colour.
Tell people what happens next after they send.

resource-scheduler.what: A timeline grid with one row per person, room or item and bookings shown as bars along a time scale. It shows who or what is free when.
uses: Assigning staff, rooms or vehicles to jobs.
Seeing a team's day at a glance.
Spotting gaps and double bookings.
avoid: A single person's calendar: use a standard calendar view.
Long lists of events without a time dimension: use a table.
practices: Keep resource names visible while scrolling sideways.
Label bars with a short title and the time.
Make the time scale and current time easy to read.
Allow horizontal scrolling on small screens rather than squeezing the grid.

shift-planner.what: A table of people against days showing each person's shifts, with totals per week. It lets managers see coverage and workload together.
uses: Planning weekly staff rotas.
Setting on-call schedules.
Checking people's hours against their contracts.
avoid: Booking rooms or equipment by the hour: use a resource timeline.
Tracking hours already worked: use a timesheet.
practices: Show totals next to contract hours and flag overtime in words and colour.
Mark weekends and days off clearly.
Distinguish shift types by label as well as colour.
Confirm before publishing the roster to staff.

booking-slot-picker.what: A way for visitors to choose a date, then pick from the free time slots on that day. Slots have a fixed length and are often grouped by morning and afternoon.
uses: Booking a call, visit or demo.
Reserving a time at a clinic, salon or service desk.
Scheduling a delivery or collection.
avoid: Choosing a date range such as a stay: use a date range picker.
Bookings that depend on service or staff: use a stepped booking flow.
practices: Show only times that can be booked, or show full ones as disabled with a reason.
Display the slot length and timezone near the slots.
Group times by part of day to shorten scanning.
Summarise the chosen time before the final confirm.

appointment-picker.what: A step-by-step booking flow: choose a service and person, then a date and time, then confirm. A running summary keeps earlier choices visible.
uses: Booking appointments where the service sets the length.
Choosing a specific staff member or location.
Reserving a time with a deposit or contact details.
avoid: One service and one person: a simple slot picker is enough.
Booking a long stay or date range: use a date range picker.
practices: Keep each step to one decision.
Show duration and price with each service.
Hold the chosen slot briefly and say how long.
Let people go back and change a choice without losing others.

conflict-resolver.what: A view that shows two bookings that overlap, side by side, and gives clear options to fix it such as moving or keeping both.
uses: Saving an event that overlaps another.
Importing a calendar or schedule with clashes.
Handling double-booked rooms or people.
avoid: Simple warnings that need no decision: use an inline message.
Preventing clashes altogether: hide or disable unavailable times.
practices: Explain exactly what clashes and when.
Show both items so they can be compared.
Offer concrete actions, including a suggested free time.
Say what will change before the person confirms.

data-table.what: A grid of rows and columns for comparing records across several attributes. It usually supports sorting, selecting rows, searching and paging.
uses: Lists of users, orders, devices or documents.
Comparing records on several fields at once.
Acting on many rows together.
avoid: Browsing items mostly by image: use a card grid.
Layout of a page: use layout elements, not a table.
Two or three simple facts per item: use a list.
practices: Give every column a clear header and a table caption.
Align numbers to the right and text to the left.
Show a helpful empty state when there are no rows.
Keep search, bulk actions and paging close to the table.

accuracy-table.what: A table comparing a measured value with a reference value, showing the difference and how close it is. Colour and words flag results that are too far off.
uses: Checking automatic counts against manual counts.
Comparing model or test runs with expected results.
Reviewing measurement quality across sites.
avoid: Showing a single score: use a progress bar or stat.
Trends over time: use a chart.
practices: Show the difference as a signed number so direction is clear.
Say what the thresholds are in a caption.
Flag poor results with a word, not only colour.
Right-align the numbers so they compare easily.

filter-bar.what: A row above a list or table that shows which filters are active, usually as removable tags, with the result count and a way to clear them all.
uses: Showing which filters narrow a list.
Letting people remove one filter at a time.
Confirming how many results match.
avoid: The filter controls themselves: use a filter panel or drawer.
Choosing one view among a few: use tabs.
practices: Show only filters that are applied.
Make each tag removable with one click.
Offer a single 'Clear all' action.
Announce the new result count to screen readers.

panel.what: A bordered section of a page with a header and a body, grouping related content into one clearly labelled block. It may have actions in a footer.
uses: Dashboard blocks such as charts or summaries.
Sections of a settings or detail page.
Grouping a form's related fields.
avoid: Wrapping every small item: too many boxes create clutter.
Content that needs to stay hidden until asked for: use an accordion.
practices: Give every panel a clear title that says what it answers.
Put actions that affect the panel in its header or footer.
Keep panels in a grid that reflows on small screens.
Avoid nesting panels inside panels.

tabbed-panel-set.what: A single box with tabs along the top that switch between related views of the same thing. Only one view shows at a time.
uses: Switching a metric between day, week and month.
Showing the same data as a chart or a table.
Splitting a detail view into a few related parts.
avoid: Steps that must happen in order: use a stepper.
Views people need to compare side by side: show them together.
practices: Keep tab labels short and clear.
Keep the content height steady so the page does not jump.
Remember the last selected tab where that helps.
Limit tabs to a handful.

card-list.what: A vertical list where each record is a card showing its name, a few key facts and actions. It reads well on narrow screens.
uses: Showing records on phones.
Browsing items with long names.
Lists where people read more than they compare.
avoid: Comparing many attributes across rows: use a table.
Image-led browsing: use a card grid.
practices: Make the whole card easy to tap.
Put the most important fact first.
Keep every card in the same layout.
Keep actions few and clearly labelled.

list-header.what: The area above a list with its title, item count, search, view options and create button. It gathers the controls that change the list.
uses: Top of a list page.
Top of a list inside a dashboard panel.
Putting search and create actions together.
avoid: Page titles with no list below: use a page header.
Complex filtering: use a filter panel.
practices: Show the count next to the title.
Keep controls in a predictable order.
Put the main create action at the end.
Stack the tools below the title on small screens.

summary-tiles.what: A row of small tiles, each showing a count for a status or group. They give a quick overview and often act as shortcuts to filter a list.
uses: Counting items by state such as online or offline.
Showing open and closed tasks.
Counting issues by severity.
avoid: Trends over time: use a chart.
Many categories: use a filter menu or a table.
practices: Put a clear label with each number.
Start with an 'All' tile.
Highlight the active tile with more than colour.
Keep to a few meaningful states.

autocomplete-results-table.what: Search results shown as you type, in a compact table with the matching text highlighted. Several attributes per result help people tell them apart.
uses: Finding records by name or code.
Telling apart similar names on different sites.
Quick lookup before opening a record.
avoid: Choosing one value from a short fixed list: use a select.
Single-field suggestions: use a plain suggestion list.
practices: Wait a moment after typing before searching.
Highlight the matching text.
Limit the rows and link to the full results.
Announce the result count to screen readers.

image.what: A picture that carries content, such as a product photo or plan. It needs a text description and reserved space so the page does not shift as it loads.
uses: Showing a product, place or person.
Illustrating a record's main details.
Showing a plan, diagram or screenshot.
avoid: Decoration with no meaning: use a background or leave it out.
Text content: use real text, not text inside an image.
practices: Write alt text that describes what matters, or leave it empty if decorative.
Set width and height so the layout does not jump.
Load below-the-fold images lazily.
Use modern, compressed formats and sensible sizes.

thumbnail.what: A small cropped preview of an image, used to recognise an item quickly in lists, tables and pickers.
uses: Previewing items in lists and tables.
Choosing between images or files.
Showing a record's picture in a card.
avoid: Viewing details of the image: link to a larger version.
Images with essential small text: show a bigger one.
practices: Use one size and crop consistently.
Leave alt text empty when the name sits beside it.
Reserve the space to avoid shifts while loading.
Make clickable thumbnails large enough to tap.

hero-image.what: A large, wide image at the top of a page that sets its mood or subject. It is common on marketing and landing pages.
uses: Opening a landing or campaign page.
Introducing a product, event or story.
Giving a section a strong visual start.
avoid: Task screens and dashboards: it pushes the task down the page.
Conveying information: use text or a chart.
practices: Choose an image that supports the message.
Make sure text over it stays readable.
Serve sizes that fit each screen.
Describe it in alt text if it carries meaning.

media-frame.what: A box that holds a fixed shape, such as 16:9 or square, for an image, video, map or chart. It reserves space before the content loads.
uses: Showing images in galleries and cards.
Embedding video, maps or charts.
Keeping a grid of mixed media neat.
avoid: Content that must show in full: use a frame that fits without cropping.
Content with its own size: no frame needed.
practices: Pick one ratio per group of items.
Decide whether to crop or fit the content.
Set the frame size before the media loads.
Always give the media a text alternative.

snapshot-image.what: A still picture taken from a video or camera, shown with where it came from and when it was captured.
uses: Showing key moments from a video.
Galleries of captured images.
Evidence or audit images that need a time.
avoid: Live or moving content: use a video frame.
Decorative pictures: use a plain image.
practices: Show the source and time on a solid background so text stays readable.
Put the time in the alt text too.
Show a clear message when an image has expired or been removed.
Keep a consistent shape across a gallery.

recording-frame.what: A video or stream frame that clearly shows it is being recorded or is live. It uses an outline and a word label so the state is hard to miss.
uses: Live camera feeds.
Screen or meeting recordings in progress.
Streams that are being stored.
avoid: Recorded clips that are not live: use a normal video frame.
General status of a thing: use a status indicator.
practices: Use a word such as 'Recording' or 'Live', not only colour.
Keep any motion subtle and respect reduced-motion settings.
Place the label where people will see it.
Remove the marker as soon as recording stops.

video-frame.what: A video player with standard controls inside a fixed-shape box. It plays recorded clips on the page.
uses: Tutorials and product demos.
Recorded meetings or clips.
Short explainers within an article.
avoid: Short looping graphics: use an animated image or an animation.
Live streams: use a live frame.
practices: Add captions for speech.
Never start playing with sound automatically.
Set a poster image and reserve the space.
Keep the browser's own controls so they work with a keyboard.

illustration.what: A simple drawing used to add friendliness to a page, usually for an empty, no-results or error state.
uses: Empty lists and first-use screens.
No search results.
Error and not-found pages.
avoid: Decorating pages that already have content.
Explaining steps in detail: use text or a diagram.
practices: Pair it with a clear title and a next action.
Keep it simple and consistent in style.
Treat it as decoration with no alt text.
Make sure it works in light and dark themes.

qr-code.what: A square barcode that a phone camera can scan to open a link or read a code. It is shown with the same text written out.
uses: Pairing a phone or device.
Linking to a web page from a printed item.
Setting up two-factor sign-in.
avoid: Links people can simply click: use a normal link.
Long text: use a short link, because dense codes scan poorly.
practices: Keep dark modules on a light background with a quiet border.
Print the text or link below as a fallback.
Make it large enough to scan.
Test it with a real phone.

barcode.what: A row of lines that a scanner reads to identify an item, with its number printed underneath.
uses: Labelling assets or inventory.
Printing tickets and passes.
Looking up items at a counter or warehouse.
avoid: Phone scanning from a screen: a QR code is easier to read.
Showing a number only: use plain text.
practices: Keep dark bars on a plain light background.
Print the digits below for people.
Leave empty space at both ends.
Test with a real scanner at the printed size.

status-dot.what: A small coloured circle next to a word showing the current state of something, such as online, offline or stopped.
uses: Showing online or offline in a list.
Showing running or stopped services.
Showing enabled or disabled items.
avoid: Statuses that need more emphasis: use a badge.
Alerts and messages: use an alert.
practices: Always pair the dot with a word.
Keep the number of colours small.
Use the same colour for the same meaning everywhere.
Use motion only for live states, and stop it for reduced motion.

badge.what: A small label with a short word that shows a status or category, such as Approved, Draft or New.
uses: Showing a record's status in a table.
Marking items as new or beta.
Showing a plan or role.
avoid: Filter choices people can click: use tags.
Showing a number: use a count badge.
Long text: use a normal label.
practices: Use one or two words.
Do not rely on colour alone.
Keep colours consistent in meaning.
Check text contrast on the background.

alert-icon.what: The symbol at the start of a message that shows its type, such as an error, warning or success.
uses: Leading an alert or banner.
Marking error and success messages in forms.
Showing the type of a notification.
avoid: Decoration with no meaning: leave it out.
Showing an item's status in a list: use a status dot or badge.
practices: Use the same symbol for the same type everywhere.
Place it in the same spot on every message.
Never rely on the icon alone, include text.
Match the symbol to the colour of the message.

count-badge.what: A small circle or pill with a number showing how many items need attention, such as unread messages or open tasks.
uses: Unread notifications on a bell icon.
Pending items on a navigation link.
Item totals on a tab.
avoid: Status words: use a badge.
Counts that never reach zero: they stop being noticed.
practices: Cap large numbers, for example 99+.
Hide the count when it is zero if that fits.
Give screen readers the meaning, such as '3 unread'.
Keep it small and placed on the corner.

tag.what: A small label for a keyword or category. Tags can be plain, clickable to filter, or removable when they show chosen values.
uses: Keywords on a record.
Active filters that can be removed.
Chosen values in a multi-select field.
avoid: Showing a status: use a badge.
Navigating between pages: use links or tabs.
practices: Keep text short.
Let people remove a tag with a clearly named button.
Show the selected state with more than colour.
Shorten long values and give the full text on hover.
